items.q: A galvanic cell is built from a Ni/Ni²⁺ half-cell and an Ag/Ag⁺ half-cell under standard conditions. Calculate E°cell.

mistakes.why: Value: you doubled E° for silver because its half-reaction is doubled. E° is intensive: balancing electrons never changes it.
Value: you added the two reduction potentials. Use E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode).
Sign: in a galvanic cell the cathode is the half-reaction with the more positive E°, so E°cell is positive.

why.correct: Silver has the more positive E°, so Ag⁺ is reduced (cathode) and Ni is oxidized (anode). E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.80 V − (−0.25 V) = 1.05 V.

items.q: Which is the balanced overall reaction for the Ni/Ag galvanic cell?
options: Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s) → Ni(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq)
Ni(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s)
Ni(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + Ag(s)
Ni(s) + 2 Ag(s) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag⁺(aq)

why.correct: Oxidation Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻; reduction 2 Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2 Ag; overall Ni + 2 Ag⁺ → Ni²⁺ + 2 Ag.
options: This is the reverse, with E° = −1.05 V: not favored, so it is not what the galvanic cell runs.
Right: nickel is oxidized, silver ions are reduced, and two Ag⁺ take the two electrons from each Ni.
Atoms balance but charge does not (+1 vs +2). Two electrons need two Ag⁺.
Both metals are oxidized here; a redox reaction needs one species reduced.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for the reaction in the Ni/Ag cell, Ni(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s).

mistakes.why: Value: n is the moles of electrons transferred in the balanced equation: 2, not 1.
Sign: ΔG° = −nFE°. A positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°.

items.q: Which pair of half-cells from the table would give the largest E°cell?
options: Al/Al³⁺ and Cu/Cu²⁺
Zn/Zn²⁺ and Ag/Ag⁺
Pb/Pb²⁺ and Mg/Mg²⁺
Mg/Mg²⁺ and Ag/Ag⁺

why.correct: E°cell is largest when the cathode has the most positive E° and the anode the most negative.
options: E°cell = 0.34 − (−1.66) = 2.00 V, less than the Mg/Ag cell.
E°cell = −0.13 − (−2.37) = 2.24 V, less than with silver as the cathode.
Right: the most positive (+0.80) minus the most negative (−2.37) gives 3.17 V.

items.q: Which species in the table is the strongest reducing agent?
options: Mg(s)
Ag⁺(aq)
Mg²⁺(aq)
Ag(s)

why.correct: A reducing agent is oxidized. The metal whose ion has the most negative E° is oxidized most readily.
options: Right: its reduction potential is the most negative, so the reverse, Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻, is the most favored oxidation.
Ag⁺ is the strongest oxidizing agent: it is the most easily reduced.
Mg²⁺ is very hard to reduce; it is the weakest oxidizing agent, not a reducing agent.
Silver is the hardest metal in the table to oxidize, so it is the weakest reducing agent.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied each E° by its coefficient (3 Cu²⁺, 2 Al). E° is intensive and is never multiplied.
Value: you added the reduction potentials. Subtract the anode’s E° from the cathode’s.

why.correct: Cu²⁺ has the more positive E°, so it is reduced; Al is oxidized. E°cell = 0.34 V − (−1.66 V) = 2.00 V. The coefficients 2 and 3 used to balance electrons do not change any E°.

items.q: How many moles of electrons, n, are transferred in the balanced equation 2 Al(s) + 3 Cu²⁺(aq) → 2 Al³⁺(aq) + 3 Cu(s)?

why.correct: n is the least common multiple of the electrons in the two half-reactions: 2 × 3 = 6.
options: That is the electrons for one Al atom. The equation has two Al atoms.
That is the electrons for one Cu²⁺ ion. The equation has three of them.
Right: 2 Al each lose 3 electrons and 3 Cu²⁺ each gain 2: six electrons.
Adding 3 and 2 does not count electrons. Multiply electrons per atom by atoms: 2 × 3 = 3 × 2 = 6.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for 2 Al(s) + 3 Cu²⁺(aq) → 2 Al³⁺(aq) + 3 Cu(s).

mistakes.why: Value: n = 6 mol e⁻ for this equation (2 Al × 3e⁻), not 2.
Value: n = 6 mol e⁻ for this equation (3 Cu²⁺ × 2e⁻), not 3.
Value: you used an E° multiplied by coefficients (4.34 V). Use E°cell = 2.00 V; the coefficients enter only through n.

items.q: A student writes E°cell = 3(+0.34) − 2(−1.66) = 4.34 V "because the equation has 3 Cu²⁺ and 2 Al." Which correction is best?
options: The coefficients should be divided, not multiplied, giving 0.34/3 + 1.66/2.
The student is right; the coefficients belong in E° and in n as well.
E° is intensive, like temperature, so coefficients never change it: E°cell = 2.00 V.
The anode’s E° alone should be multiplied, because electrons are released there.

why.correct: E° is energy per coulomb. Balancing electrons changes the total energy (through n in ΔG° = −nFE°) but not the energy per coulomb.
options: Coefficients do not enter E° at all, whether multiplied or divided.
The coefficients affect n (and so ΔG°), but never E°.
Right: potential is energy per unit charge; doubling the reaction doubles both, leaving E° unchanged.
Neither E° is multiplied.

items.q: For a redox reaction at standard conditions, which set of signs goes together?
options: E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0, K > 1
E°cell > 0, ΔG° > 0, K < 1
E°cell < 0, ΔG° < 0, K > 1
E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0, K < 1

why.correct: ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −RT ln K, so E° > 0 ⇔ ΔG° < 0 ⇔ K > 1.
options: Right: a positive cell potential means a favored reaction with products favored at equilibrium.
ΔG° = −nFE°: positive E° gives negative ΔG°.
A negative E°cell gives a positive ΔG° and K < 1.
A negative ΔG° gives K > 1 (ΔG° = −RT ln K).

items.q: For Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Zn(s), E° = −1.10 V. What does this tell you?
options: The reaction is favored but slow, so it needs a catalyst.
The cell will run with electrons flowing from Zn to Cu, so it is still galvanic.
The reaction is at equilibrium, because E° is negative.
It is not favored; it needs an electrolytic cell with a power supply.

why.correct: A negative E°cell means ΔG° = −nFE° > 0. The reaction can be driven by a power supply, which is an electrolytic cell.
options: A negative E° means not favored; a catalyst cannot change that.
For this reaction as written, copper would be oxidized; with E° < 0 that does not happen on its own.
At equilibrium the cell potential E is zero, not E°.
Right: a negative E°cell means ΔG° > 0, so the reaction must be driven.

items.q: For Cu(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s), E° = +0.46 V at 298 K. Calculate K. (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

mistakes.why: Value: n = 2 mol e⁻ for this equation (one Cu gives two electrons).

items.q: A galvanic cell made from a metal M in 1.0 M M²⁺ and Cu in 1.0 M Cu²⁺ has E°cell = 0.74 V. M is the anode. E° for Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V. Calculate the standard reduction potential of M²⁺/M.

mistakes.why: Value: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), so E°(anode) = 0.34 − 0.74, not 0.34 + 0.74.
Sign: M is the anode, so its reduction potential is lower than copper’s.

items.q: Reaction 1 is Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), with E° = 1.10 V and ΔG° = −212 kJ/mol. Reaction 2 is the same reaction with every coefficient doubled. What are E° and ΔG° for Reaction 2?

why.correct: ΔG° = −nFE°: doubling the equation doubles n (2 → 4) but not E°, so ΔG° doubles.
options: E° does not double when the equation is doubled.
Right: E° is intensive and stays the same; ΔG° is extensive (n doubles from 2 to 4) and doubles.
Doubling both E° and n would quadruple ΔG°. Neither is right: E° stays 1.10 V.
ΔG° depends on the amount of reaction: twice the equation, twice the free energy.

items.q: Use these standard reduction potentials: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Ni²⁺/Ni −0.25 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V. Which reactions are thermodynamically favored under standard conditions? Select ALL that apply.
options: Zn(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Ni(s)
Cu(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ni(s)
Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Zn(s)
2 Ag(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → 2 Ag⁺(aq) + Zn(s)

why.correct: For each reaction, E° = E°(species reduced) − E°(species oxidized). Only the zinc-nickel reaction gives a positive value.

items.q: In ΔG° = −nFE°, what does n stand for?
options: The moles of electrons transferred in the balanced overall equation
The number of moles of metal that plate out at the cathode
The number of half-reactions in the cell, which is 2
The charge on the cation formed at the anode

why.correct: n is the moles of electrons transferred per mole of reaction as written.
options: Right: n counts electrons in the reaction as written, so ΔG° scales with the equation.
This equals n only when each ion gains one electron; n counts electrons, not atoms.
n is a count of electrons transferred, which can be 1, 2, 6 or more.
This equals n only if one anode atom reacts; for 2 Al → 2 Al³⁺, n = 6.
